reason: The sources provide enough overlapping details on the discovery, dimensions, and atmospheric studies of GJ 1214 b to support a 45-second script.
story: Discovered in December 2009 by the MEarth Project, exoplanet GJ 1214 b orbits a red dwarf star roughly 40 to 48 light-years away in the constellation Ophiuchus. Roughly six to eight times the mass of Earth and about 2.7 times its radius, this mini-Neptune completely lacks a counterpart in our solar system. For over a decade, astronomers were stumped by a thick layer of haze or clouds hiding its true nature. Early Hubble observations suggested a steamy water-world. However, recent observations using the James Webb Space Telescope's MIRI instrument mapped the planet's day and night sides, revealing massive temperature swings from 535 to 326 degrees Fahrenheit. This intense heat and heavy molecular signatures ruled out a primordial hydrogen atmosphere, pointing instead toward a heavy, metal-rich, or carbon-dioxide-dominated atmosphere resembling a super-Venus.
angle: A scorching hot mini-Neptune hidden behind a thick, mysterious shroud of haze that turned out to have a metal-rich, super-Venus atmosphere rather than a simple water ocean.

claims.claim: GJ 1214 b was discovered in December 2009.
The exoplanet was discovered by the MEarth Project.
GJ 1214 b is located approximately 40 to 48 light-years from Earth.
The planet is located in the constellation Ophiuchus.
GJ 1214 b has a radius about 2.7 times that of Earth.
The mass of GJ 1214 b is roughly 6 to 8 times that of Earth.
The planet's atmosphere was hidden for over a decade by a thick layer of clouds or haze.
Researchers used the James Webb Space Telescope and its MIRI instrument to study the planet's atmosphere.
JWST observations revealed dayside temperatures reaching around 535 degrees Fahrenheit (279 degrees Celsius).
JWST observations revealed nightside temperatures dropping to around 326 degrees Fahrenheit (165 degrees Celsius).
The parent star of GJ 1214 b is a red dwarf.
The planet orbits its star in approximately 1.5 to 1.6 Earth days.

disputed: Whether the planet is a true water-world, a mini-Neptune, or a carbon-dioxide/metal-rich super-Venus. The script should attribute these shifting theories to changing scientific studies over time, noting that early data pointed toward steam or water while newer JWST findings point to heavy metal and carbon dioxide components.
